Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

Source: vignettes/cosmos.Rmd
cosmos.Rmd

Read Cosmos DB documents in a Shiny app using each visitor’s Microsoft Entra account and Cosmos DB data permissions. oauth_db_cosmos_api() runs NoSQL queries over HTTPS, collects result pages and returns data frames. You can also read one document or fetch one result page at a time.

This guide covers Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL. MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin and Table endpoints use other protocols. Cosmos DB in Microsoft Fabric hasn’t been validated with this backend.

Prepare the account and sign-in

You need an existing Cosmos DB for NoSQL account, database and container. Copy the account’s URI from the Azure portal, such as https://example.documents.azure.com. Supply database and container IDs separately; don’t use an account key or connection string.

Register a Web application in Microsoft Entra with your Shiny app’s exact redirect URI. The example uses http://localhost:8100. Use the registration’s tenant ID, application ID and server-side client secret. The shared registration guide explains those settings and production redirect URIs.

oauth_db_cosmos_client() requests openid, profile, offline_access and https://cosmos.azure.com/.default. Cosmos DB doesn’t expose a delegated permission in the app-registration permission picker; don’t invent a user_impersonation permission. Your tenant and application registration must allow obtaining a user access token for this resource. Validate that combination before deploying: the offline checks do not establish tenant consent or live browser sign-in.

Assign each visitor a Cosmos DB data-plane role, such as Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader, scoped to the required database or container. Subscription Reader, Contributor and account-management roles alone don’t grant document access. Follow Microsoft’s data-plane RBAC guide to create the assignments. The app doesn’t create databases, containers, role assignments or users.

Set these values in your environment or .Renviron, then restart R:

OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID=your-tenant-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-application-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
OAUTHDB_COSMOS_URL=https://example.documents.azure.com
OAUTHDB_DATABASE=reporting
OAUTHDB_COSMOS_CONTAINER=orders

Install shinyOAuthDB using the installation instructions. Install jsonlite too. This backend doesn’t need ODBC, Python, Azure CLI or an Azure SDK.

Build an app

This example reads up to 20 documents with id, country and total fields. Change the query and partition key to match your container. Save it as app.R and run it in R:

pkgs <- c("shiny", "shinyOAuth", "shinyOAuthDB", "mirai", "jsonlite")
for (pkg in pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
}

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

client <- oauth_db_cosmos_client(
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE, async = TRUE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  cosmos <- oauth_db_cosmos_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv(
      "OAUTHDB_COSMOS_URL",
      "https://example.documents.azure.com"
    ),
    database = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_DATABASE"),
    container = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_COSMOS_CONTAINER", "orders")
  )
  query_task <- oauth_db_task(cosmos)
  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke(
      "SELECT TOP 20 c.id, c.total FROM c WHERE c.country = @country",
      parameters = list(country = "NL"),
      partition_key = "NL"
    )
  })
  output$rows <- renderTable(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)
    onStop(function() mirai::daemons(0))
  }),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)
# Open http://localhost:8100 in your regular browser.

Create the API client inside server() and pass auth$connection without parentheses. Sign in and click Load rows to fetch in a background worker. Cosmos DB checks the visitor’s token and applies their data-plane roles. The output clears on sign-out or account replacement; click Load rows again to fetch for the new account.

Queries and documents

Use @name placeholders in SQL and a named list without @ in parameters. Values are sent separately from the query:

cosmos$query(
  "SELECT c.id, c.total FROM c WHERE c.total >= @minimum",
  parameters = list(minimum = 100),
  partition_key = "NL"
)

document <- cosmos$read("order-123", partition_key = "NL")
document$total

Objects become data-frame columns. Nested objects, arrays and mixed types stay in list columns. Missing and null fields become NA in scalar columns. Large JSON integers stay as strings. For exact decimal identifiers or money, store and project strings; Cosmos DB’s JSON numbers don’t supply arbitrary decimal precision.

SELECT VALUE can return scalars, arrays or objects. Scalar or mixed results use a value list column. Empty queries return a data frame with no field schema. To retain native JSON lists and distinguish missing fields from explicit nulls, use raw = TRUE or $query_page().

Partition keys and access rules

Omitting partition_key enables a cross-partition query. Supply a scalar to target one logical partition. For a hierarchical partition key, pass the components in their configured order, such as list("NL", "Retail"). Use list(NULL) for a JSON null partition key. Point reads require a key.

The client uses the REST gateway and doesn’t implement the vendor SDK’s query-plan distribution and result merging. Some cross-partition aggregates or ordered queries need an SDK; use a partition-specific query where possible. Unsupported queries return an error from the service.

A partition key or SQL filter is a query choice, not an access rule. Cosmos DB RBAC controls access to databases and containers, not individual documents selected by your SQL filter. Give visitors access only to the containers they are allowed to read.

Result pages, usage and failures

$query() collects every result page within one timeout, including empty pages that carry a continuation token. A page uses a current access token but stays bound to the account that started the operation. It stops if that authorization is replaced or revoked. The client carries Cosmos DB session tokens between pages of the operation.

Use raw = TRUE to inspect the total request charge, measured in request units, alongside the collected documents. Queries can incur charges even if fetching a later page fails. For larger results, fetch one page at a time:

first <- cosmos$query_page(
  "SELECT c.id, c.total FROM c",
  partition_key = "NL"
)
first$documents
first$request_charge

if (!is.null(first$continuation)) {
  second <- cosmos$query_page(
    "SELECT c.id, c.total FROM c",
    partition_key = "NL",
    continuation = first$continuation,
    session_token = first$session_token
  )
}

Reuse a continuation only with the same query, parameters, partition and account. Clear saved pages and continuation tokens on sign-out or account replacement. The shared session guide covers saved results and background fetching.

Each read can refresh and retry once after HTTP 401. HTTP 403, throttling (429), redirects and other failures stop the operation. There is no automatic retry for throttling, and no fallback to a key, managed identity or the hosting machine’s account. Errors omit service response bodies and credentials.

The sign-in helper uses the separate cosmos token target and the documented .default consent scope. An existing shinyOAuth authorization can be used with target = NULL or another named target if it obtains a token accepted by the account. For another Azure cloud, supply the proper resource and Microsoft provider explicitly; the preset defaults to Azure public cloud.

Validation boundary

Offline tests exercise real shinyOAuth authorization references and HTTP request construction with synthetic tokens. They cover pagination, partition keys, JSON values, current tokens, account changes, sign-out, timeouts and sanitized failures. They don’t validate live Entra consent, Cosmos DB RBAC or a cloud account. The backend notes record the implementation decision and remaining live checks.
